iii ABSTRACT

Dr. Douglas C. Neckers, Advisor

The practical uses of pentacene, the most promising polyacene in the area of

organic field-effect transistors, are limited by its sensitivity to oxygen and poor solubility

in organic solvents.  To overcome these disadvantages, new organic semiconductors,

2,3,6,9,10,13-hexa(trimethylsilylethynyl)pentacene, 2,3,9,10-

tetrakis(triisopropylsilylethynyl)-6,13-bis(trimethylsilylethynyl)pentacene, and 2,3,9,10-

tetrakis(3,5-di-t-butylphenylethynyl)-6,13-bis(trimethylsilylethynyl)pentacene were

designed, synthesized, and fully characterized.

In comparison with pentacene, they are stable and soluble and have extended π-

conjugation. Each demonstrates reduction potentials that are essentially unchanged, but

different oxidation potentials. The HOMO-LUMO gaps estimated from the

electrochemical data are ca. 1.7 eV, which is among the lowest HOMO-LUMO gaps

reported in the literature for pentacene derivatives. The compounds fluoresce in the deep

red region, with the width at half height being less than 40 nm. In thin films the

compounds show strong aggregation and adopt a favorable stacking geometry with the

molecular long axis upright to the substrate surface.

Modifying pentacene at the central and terminal rings with ethynyl moieties

proves viable in synthesizing new pentacene derivatives and tuning their electronic

properties. The three new pentacene derivatives may be useful for electronic devices such

as organic field-effect transistors or organic light-emitting diodes.

## CHAPTER 1.   INTRODUCTION

Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) attract continuous interest as the most widely

studied organic π-conjugated materials for optoelectronic applications (light-emitting diodes,

field-effect transistors, photovoltaics, etc.). Linear PAHs, composed of laterally fused benzene

rings, are called linear acenes or simply acenes. Particular attention has been given to linear

acenes due to their importance as organic semiconductors. Pentacene (Chart 1.1), a simple linear

acene consisting of five fused benzene rings, has emerged as a viable candidate for the charge

transport layer in organic field-effect transistors (OFETs). OFETs are being developed for

potential applications in active-matrix displays as switching devices and in low-end data storage

systems. The interest in pentacene, which exhibits p-type transport, stems primarily from its

relatively high hole mobility and high on-to-off current ratio in OFETs.1-6 The practical uses of

pentacene are limited by its insolubility, instability and herringbone packing in solid state.

### 1.2.   Solid State Properties of Pentacene and Its Derivatives

In the solid state, PAHs are structurally planar or near planar and lack conformational

flexibility because planar conformations can be packed more densely than twisted or nonplanar

ones. Acenes from benzene30 to pentacene31-33 all adopt the herringbone motif in their crystal

structures (Figure 1.1), in which the edge of one molecule is oriented toward the face of another

with only a minimal π-stacking (edge-to-face interaction).34 In general, aromatic hydrocarbons

show a great propensity to polymorphism. Indeed, several pentacene polymorphs are known and

complete X-ray data are available for these structures.34-37 It was suggested that the sample purity

or the growth temperature not the crystal growth method (from solution or vapor) are possible

determining factors in obtaining a given polymorph.38 Calculations indicated that the electronic

energy gaps for different polymorph structures vary slightly. Intermolecular interactions are

more favorable in the vapor-phase grown structure.39 The structure of a monolayer-thick

pentacene film grown on amorphous silicon dioxide was studied by grazing-angle incidence X-

the long axis perpendicular to the SiO2 substrate. Emulation based on the cell parameters

obtained with GI-XRD reveals that in the monolayer pentacene molecules pack in herringbone

motif similar to that observed in the bulk.

Chemical modification of pentacene was utilized in attempts to discourage herringbone

packing. Isopropyl-substituted pentacenes show significant overlap of the pentacene rings in

adjacent molecules. 6,13-Bis(triisopropylsilylethynyl)pentacene stacks in two-dimensional

columnar arrays.  Unsymmetrical 5,14-bis(triisopropylsilylethynyl)pentacene forms nearly

perfect stacked pairs, with the solubilizing groups arranged to minimize steric interactions.

Unfortunately, these pairs then pack in a herringbone pattern similar to that observed for pristine

pentacene.41 The crystal structure of 2,3,9,10-tetramethylpentacene and perfluoropentacene

shows the herringbone packing similar to that of pentacene.42,43 5,7,12,14-Tetraphenylpentacene

was first prepared in 1942 using Grignard reagent.20 Its crystal structure,  which did not show

any π-stacking or herringbone structure, was elucidated recently.44 It may be noted that the

ability for self-assembly of the aromatic moieties into π-stacked arrays can be induced by

disrupting edge-to-face interactions. Substitution at the center peri positions of pentacene with a

relatively bulky group proved effective, given careful selection of the specific group. If the group

is attached directly to the acene, π-stacking interactions may be disrupted, as in the case of

5,7,12,14-tetraphenylpentacene; if the group is too small, edge-to-face interactions will not be

affected and herringbone packing will occur, as in the case of perfluoropentacene. Separating the

substituent from the core by a rigid alkyne spacer turned out to be a good option.

### 1.3.   OFET Performances of Pentacene and Its Derivatives

The first descriptions of the field effect in organic semiconductors date back to 1970.45-47

Despite extensive work, OFETs minimally impacted optoelectronic applications until the late

1980’s, when an OFET based on electrochemically polymerized polythiophene was first


<!-- Page 21 -->


6

reported.48,49 The OFETs were continuously improved afterwards and were identified as potential

elements in electronic devices. Currently, the most developed OFETs are based on pentacene.

A field-effect transistor (FET) is the type of transistor commonly used for weak-signal

amplification. The device can amplify analog or digital signals and act as a DC switch or an

oscillator. In the FET, the current flows along a semiconductor path called the channel. At one

end of the channel there is an electrode called the source.  At the other end of the channel, there

is an electrode called the drain. The physical diameter of the channel is fixed, but its effective

electrical diameter can be varied by the application of a voltage to a control electrode called the

gate. The conductivity of the FET depends, at any given instant in time, on the effective

electrical diameter of the channel. A small change in gate voltage can cause a large variation in

the current from the source to the drain. This is how the FET amplifies signals. Most of today's

FETs are "MOSFETs", or metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistors, where the channel

can be either a N-type or P-type semiconductor. The gate electrode is a piece of metal insulated

from the channel by a thin oxide layer. Because the oxide layer acts as a dielectric, there is

essentially no current between the gate and the channel at any time during the signal cycle. The

most popular modern MOSFETs are silicon-based thin-film transistors. In this case, the channel

is the amorphous silicon and the charge-carrier mobility ranges from 0.5 to 1 cm2/V·s.

Almost all the OFETs in the literature are MOSFETs. The channel of OFETs is made of

organic semiconductors instead of amorphous silicon. There are two basic types of OFET

architecture: bottom-contact (Figure 1.2) and top-contact (Figure 1.3). In the bottom-contact

architecture the gate electrode is first laid down, on which a silicon oxide layer is thermally

grown. Source and drain electrodes are deposited on this insulating layer by conventional

microlithographic techniques. Depositing the semiconductor film is the last step. In the top-


<!-- Page 22 -->

contact architecture, the last two steps revert, resulting in source and drain electrodes on the top.

For benchmark studies, SiO2 is by far the most common inorganic insulator, but others (Si3N4,

Al2O3, etc.) have also been used.50 Recently, a significant amount of effort has been invested in

depositing the organic semiconductor onto polymeric insulators with the ultimate goal of creating

all-organic transistors.51

These two basic assemblies account for the majority of the OFETs reported in the

literature. They can be classified as bottom-gate structures, because the organic semiconductor is

deposited directly on the insulator, which is on top of the gate. In such architectures the insulator

functions not only as a dielectric but also as a substrate for the organic semiconductor film to

grow on. The insulator morphology profoundly affects the crystallinity of the organic

semiconductor thin film and thus its electronic properties.52  Fabricating the transistor on top of

the organic thin film, i.e., top-gate structure, is an alternative but double-edged option. This top-


<!-- Page 23 -->


8

gate technique automatically encapsulates the device and thus improves the air stability,53 but the

semiconductor-insulator interface in this geometry is dictated by the organic thin film and is

typically much worse than that in the bottom-gate assembly. Furthermore, the subsequent

deposition of the dielectric material can either damage or unintentionally dope the underlying

organic semiconductor, both of which are detrimental to the Ion/Ioff ratio. The Ion/Ioff ratio refers

to the ratio between the source-drain currents when a gate voltage is switched on or off. The high

Ion/Ioff ratio of >106 required in practice can only be achieved if the pristine semiconductor

contains a very small number of charge carriers. As a consequence, the material needs to be

extremely pure.

The charge transport mobility of a semiconductor is another important parameter that

determines the device performance. The charge transport mobility provides a measure of how

easily electrons or holes drift through a semiconductor in response to an electric field. Pentacene

is a p-type semiconductor, i.e., the charge carriers are preferably holes. The energy required for

the structural relaxation in pentacene (the reorganization energy), going from the neutral state to

the cation radical and the reverse, is small;54 hence, hole transport through pentacene films is

effective. The field-effect mobility in pentacene-based OFETs has been improved to equal that of

hydrogenated amorphous silicon (1 cm2/V·s) and to supersede it up to 3 cm2/V·s.2,4,5   More

recently, an even higher mobility of 5 cm2/V·s was reported for pentacene.6 A field-effect

The macroscopic properties of a material are affected not only by the properties of the

individual molecules but also by their spatial arrangement in the solid state. The high mobility

above is also correlated with the formation of large single-crystal domains in these devices and

the high degree of molecular ordering that it implies. Structural analysis of pentacene thin films


<!-- Page 24 -->


9

in these devices has shown that the molecules are packed more or less edge-to-face in two-

dimensional (2-D) layers. In the thin film, transport occurs by hopping between local states and

the charge mobility is strongly modulated by the molecular packing. The hopping rate constant is

increased with decreased distance and increased π-orbital overlap between neighboring

molecules. Although the highest mobility is in the 2-D layers, the edge-to-face packing

minimizes π-π overlap between adjacent molecules. As a result, higher mobility might be

achieved by designing conjugated molecules that stack face-to-face (π-stack) in the solid state,

thus increasing the intermolecular interaction while maintaining the desirable 2-D character of

the herringbone structure.

Pentacene-based OFETs have seen great advances during the past several years. Quite

interestingly, performance improvement was achieved mainly through optimizing the device

fabrication techniques57-59 instead of designing new materials, as was the case with the

based OFETs by chemical modification have been reported.41-43,60 For example, a mobility of 0.4

### 2.1.   Background

Organic electronics is a burgeoning industry. Extensive research in this field is

dominantly driven by the attractive characteristics of organic materials, such as low-cost

production, mechanical flexibility, and large area coverage. These are not easily achieved with

established silicon technologies. The inherent “tunability” of organic materials adds to the

advantages. Compared with their inorganic counterparts, organic materials present a unique

possibility to tune their electronic, optical, thermal, physical and mechanical properties by subtle

modification of the chemical structure. The effect of chemical design on materials’ properties

was dramatized by the spectacular development of conventional polymers in our everyday life

and is widely utilized in electronic devices as well. However, this is not true for the workhorse of

organic field effect transistors, pentacene. Extensive studies on pentacene focus on maximizing

orbital overlap in the solid state by inducing order in films. The efforts so far rely predominantly

on substrate modification, rather than on pentacene functionalization, to achieve the desired

goals.

Organic semiconductors have been studied for more than half a century,1,2 but initial

applications were limited to photoconductive properties in xerography. It was in the late 1980’s

that their broader potential in optoelectronics became clear with the demonstration of the

Organic Light Emitting Diode (OLED)3,4 and the Organic Field Effect Transistor (OFET).5-7

Pentacene was first synthesized in 1929.8 However, the 20th century passed without many


<!-- Page 32 -->


17

additional derivatives of pentacene reported (Chart 2.1 and 2.2). The short history of the use of

pentacene as an active material in OFETs,9 combined with its instability, is said to be the reason

for the relatively small pool of pentacene derivatives.

Unlike its lower molecular homologues, which are stable (e.g., benzene, naphthalene,

anthracene and tetracene), and easily extracted from coal, pentacene can be obtained only by

multi-step synthesis. In solution, it is remarkably unstable and participates actively in Diels-

Alder reactions. Under the influence of light and air (O2), reactions that oxidize pentacene will

occur preferentially at the central positions. In the solid state, pentacene is only moderately stable

to oxygen and, as well, it is considerably unstable to light.10 Pentacene also has a very high

melting point and is virtually insoluble, even in hot aromatic solvents. These self-complicating

disadvantages hinder practical applications of pentacene.

Pentacene displays the highest charge mobility among all the OFET semiconductors. It is

therefore attractive to chemically modify the pentacene core to achieve improved solubility and

stability while simultaneously maintaining or even enhancing the favorable crystal packing

geometry and orientation. Anthony et al. reported functionalizing the center ring with

trialkylsilylethynyl moieties. This not only imparted solubility to the pentacene derivatives but

also enhanced π-stacking in solid state.11-13 Introducing substituents on the 2, 3, 9, and 10

positions of the terminal rings variously affects the properties.10,14-16 These substituents include

methyl, halo, cyano, trimethylsilyl and alkoxy, but carbon-carbon triple bond previously has

never been used to functionalize the terminal rings of the pentacene core. This very triple bond

has been incorporated into conjugated polymers to act as a rigid spacer and to lengthen

conjugation.

### 2.2.   Purpose of Chemical Modification of Pentacene

To realize the modification of pentacene, an eight-step synthetic scheme (Scheme 2.1)

was designed. Modifying a pentacene core has multiple purposes and is expected to:

• increase solubility and thus simplify purification and processing,

• enable pentacene cores to self-assemble into π-stacked arrays to enhance

intermolecular orbital overlap, and

• tune the electronic properties.

We anticipated that all of the above goals might be accomplished by attaching ethynyl

groups on both the central and terminal rings. The target molecules are multi-ethynylated

symmetrical pentacenes (Chart 2.3 and Scheme 2.1). Trimethylsilyl, triisopropylsilyl and

dodecoxy are strong solublizing moieties and will definitely improve the target molecules’

solubility in common organic solvents. The carbon-carbon triple bond will push the bulky ends

away from the pentacene core, and allow the close contact between pentacene cores.

### 2.3.   Synthetic Scheme for Novel Derivatives of Pentacene

### 2.3.1.   General Description

The eight-step synthetic scheme (Scheme 2.1) involves the sequential phthalaldehyde

synthesis (steps i-iv), terminal substituent attachment (step v), ring synthesis (step vi), and

central substituent attachment (steps vii and viii). By starting with commercially available

phthalimide 2.1, iodization24 and subsequent hydrolysis yielded the desired 4,5-diiodobenzene-

1,2-dicarboxylic acid 2.3 in moderate yield (65%) on a scale of tens of grams. Via BH3 reduction,

2.3 was converted to dimethanol 2.4, which was then oxidized to the corresponding compound

2.5 in good yield through a modification of a procedure reported in the literature.18 Sonogashira

coupling25 between 2.5 and four different terminal alkynes led to 2.6a-d. A subsequent 4-fold

aldol condensation between ethynylated phthalaldehydes and 1,4-cyclohexanedione26 was

efficient in yielding pentacenequinones (100% to 60%). Pentacenequinones were converted to

the corresponding dihydropentacenediols using a standard ethynylation approach.11,27,28 To avoid

purifying final products at the last step, the dihydropentacenediols were separated and purified to

the extent that they passed elemental analysis prior to their subsequent use. This strategy turned

out to be practical and produced pentacenes 2.9a-c of good quality. Up to now, we have failed to

separate 2.9d, in that it was unstable and decomposed during workup. A similar report was

documented by Anthony et al. in attempts to prepare acyclic ethers of pentacene derivatives.13

Probably the oxygen lone electron pairs contribute to the π–conjugation and lower the oxidation

potential to an unfavorable extent.

32-63 m) and silica gel plates (200 m) were purchased from Sorbent Technologies. Reactions

that required anhydrous conditions were carried out under argon in oven-dried glassware.

Isopropyl magnesium chloride in THF was titrated with menthol prior to each use.35

The photodegradation / photooxidation of pentacene is considered to be related to the

LUMO energy level, and the possible mechanism is depicted in Figure 3.11.17,21, 22 To a first-

### 3.3.   Conclusion

Novel derivatives of pentacene 2.9a-c are strongly absorbing and moderately fluorescent

compounds. Their length of conjugation is comparable to that of hexacene, but each shows

improved stability over pentacene. They are electrochemically stable and possess higher

oxidation and lower reduction potentials than pentacene. In thin films, they demonstrate

appreciable π-stacking and ability to form films of good quality. The above advantages combined

with their solubility in common organic solvents make them promising materials for organic

electronics.

Attaching ethynyl moieties to pentacene turned out to be a good method for pentacene

modification. By doing so, not only the HOMO-LUMO gap can be tuned, but the HOMO and

LUMO energy modified. By utilizing more electron-withdrawing or donating functionalities

together with an ethynyl bridge, new materials with smaller bandgap and lower LUMO energy

can be expected.

### 4.3.1.   Solvatochromism and Intramolecular Charge Transfer

It is well known that UV-vis absorption spectra of chemical compounds may be

influenced by the surrounding medium and that the solvent can bring about a change in the

position, intensity, and shape of absorption bands. This phenomenon is termed solvatochromism.

The change in the absorption bands is often accompanied by a change in the polarity of the

medium. There are two kinds of solvatochromism: hypsochromic shift and bathochromic shift. A

hypsochromic shift is a shift of a spectral band to a higher frequency (a shorter wavelength),

referred to as a blue shift, with increasing solvent polarity. It is also called negative

solvatochromism. A bathochromic shift is a shift of a spectral band to a lower frequency (a

longer wavelength), referred to as a red shift, with increasing solvent polarity. It is also called

positive solvatochromism. Solvatochromism also exists in fluorescence spectra, i.e. the position

of emission bands is also solvent dependent. Bathochromic shifts are sometimes accompanied by

a decrease in the quantum yield of the fluorophore.

Compounds 4.2-4.6 are strongly absorbing in the UV region, evidenced by their large

molar extinction coefficients. Their absorption spectra are almost independent of solvents,

however, their fluorescence spectra exhibit significant positive solvatochromism, i.e., the

fluorescence maxima shift to the red with increasing solvent polarity. This indicates that the

solvent polarity has a smaller effect on the absorption than on the emission spectra. For example,

compound 4.5 has a red shift of 87 nm in the fluorescence spectrum recorded in acetonitrile


<!-- Page 88 -->

by 3 nm to the blue.

The significant positive solvatochromism definitely indicates that the molecules become

more polar in the excited states than in the ground state and are stabilized more by polar solvents

than by non-polar solvents. As a result, the molecules fluoresce at lower energy when the solvent

polarity increases. This stabilization is depicted in Figure 4.2.

### 4.3.3.   Two-Photon- Excited (TPE) Fluorescence

Quite interestingly, 4.1 showed TPE fluorescence whereas other compounds 4.2-4.6 did

not, under the same instrumental conditions. The reason is unclear.

The process of two-photon absorption (TPA) is similar to ordinary one-photon absorption

(OPA).  In TPA an electron absorbs two photons at approximately the same time (or within less

than a nanosecond) and achieves an excited state that corresponds to the sum of the energy of the

absorbed photons.   The molecule does not need to reach an intermediate state before arriving at

the final excited state; instead, it is excited to a "virtual state," which need not correspond to any

electronic or vibrational energy state (Figure 4.11).   Through TPA we can populate high energy

levels that are otherwise unreachable by OPA from the ground state.

For TPA, the transition probability per unit time, or cross-section, is proportional to the

square of the radiation intensity. TPA may be detected either by direct absorbance measurement

or indirectly by fluorescence. The fluorescing state gets populated by the non-radiative decay of

the TPE state and thus lies below the two-photon energy level.

In recent years, there has been a lot of  research on organic molecules which show strong

TPE fluorescence.36-40 If a two-photon excitation is carried out by a tightly focused laser beam,

the TPE fluorescence can be confined in a small volume in the order of λ3. Thus, blue TPE

fluorescence at short wavelength will have high spatial resolution for various photonic

applications, such as three-dimensional optical data storage,37 two-photon laser scanning


<!-- Page 98 -->


83

fluorescence microscopy38 and microfabrication.39 Unfortunately, most reported TPE

fluorescence to date is in the green-to-red region (500-700 nm). New organic blue TPE

fluorescence emitters are highly desirable.

*Figure 4.11.   The Jablonski diagram of OPA and TPA and fluorescence.*

In our experiment, TPE fluorescence was recorded. In acetonitrile, 4.1 fluoresces at 486

nm when excited at 428 nm. When excited at 768 nm, the emission maximum shifts to a lower

energy (491 nm). Figure 4.12 shows this appreciable difference. It is well known that the

emission is independent of the mode of the transition, i.e., OPA or TPA, and that the energy

difference in the spectra is solely due to self-absorption in concentrated solution.35,41 The

shoulder peak in the OPE fluorescence spectrum grows and becomes an obvious peak in the TPE

fluorescence spectrum. In spite of marginal differences, the OPE and TPE fluorescence spectra

match well. Photons of 1.61 eV (768 nm) are in the vicinity of half the HOMO-LUMO gap (2.55

eV, 486 nm). The TPA is believed to take place. This is also supported by the quadratic

dependency of the emission intensity on the incident laser intensity shown in Figure 4.13, which

is a characteristic of TPE fluorescence. Since the fluorescence intensity is linearly proportional to

the square of the incident laser intensity, plotting log (fluorescence intensity) against log

(incident laser intensity ) should produce a straight line with a slope of 2. In Figure 4.13, the

linear fitting has a slope of 1.65, which indicates TPA with linear interference. The TPA cross-

section estimated from the TPE fluorescence is 124 ± 5 GM for 4.1.

The X-ray crystal structure of 2.9b (Figure S.1) confirms its chemical structure (C76 H110

Si6). The conjugated skeleton is nearly planar. The five aromatic rings plus the six carbon-carbon

triple bonds are planar within +/- 0.090 Å. The two trimethylsilyl groups at 6, 13 positions

assume staggered conformation and reduce 2.9b to a C2h symmetry.

The single bonds located between triple bonds and the pentacene ring, for example, C1-

C12, are ca. 1.43 Å in length. They are significantly shorter than typical carbon-carbon single

bonds, for example C33-C35, which is 1.54 Å long. The triple bonds are 1.20 Å long in average.

Theoretical calculation at the level of DFT/B3LYP with the 6-31G** basis set in

GAUSSIAN W03 is known to predict bond lengths in excellent agreement with experimental

values.1,2 A calculation at this level was performed on 1,2-diethynylbenzene.  The bond lengths

of its triple and single bonds are found 1.21 and 1.43 Å, respectively (Figure S.2). Obviously, the

bonds in 2.9b mentioned above possess the same feature as those in 1,2-diethynylbenzene.

## S.2.    Experimental

Figure S.5.  The blue crystal of 2.9b on a glass fiber.

Dark turquoise-almost black-crystals were obtained from a benzene solution of 2.9b. A

crystal, 0.26 × 0.25 × 0.25 mm in size, was mounted on a 0.1 mm glass fiber with oil (Figure

S.5). The crystal was cooled to 120 K using an Oxford Cryostream 600 low-temperature device.

Crystal data were collected with a Bruker platform diffractometer equipped with a Smart6000

detector (graphite-monochromated, MoKα = 0.071073 nm).

The crystal was identified as a non-merohedral twin using RLATT. Two orientation

matrices were assigned to the two different twin components (GEMINI 1.02). Integration of the

data with SAINT 6.29A using both orientation matrices deconvoluted the data set into

overlapped reflections and reflections originated by only one of the twin components. Correction

for absorption, decay and inhomogeneity of the X-ray beam were applied using TWINABS. The

twinning law is a 180 º rotation around a, the ratio of the two twin components was refined to

0.364(1) : 0.636(1).

A partial structure solution was obtained by direct methods, and the remaining non-hydrogen

atoms were located with difference-Fourier techniques. All non-hydrogen atoms were refined

with anisotropic atomic displacement parameters, with the exception of the carbon atom C15,

which is disordered and was refined isotropically.  The hydrogen atoms were calculated on

idealized positions and included in the refinement as constrained atoms.  The isotropic atomic

displacement factors of the hydrogen atoms were constrained to the Ueq of the atom attached to it.

The refinements by full matrix least squares on F2 were performed with all reflections using
